# Methodological Tensions in Staggered Difference-in-Differences: Estimator Design, Assumptions, Adoption, and the Pre-Trends Problem

## 1. The Goodman-Bacon Critique and the Scale of the Problem

Goodman-Bacon's decomposition theorem (*Journal of Econometrics* 225(2): 254–277, 2021; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445) shows that the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) DiD coefficient under staggered adoption "equals a weighted average of all possible two-group/two-period DD estimators in the data." Three features of this decomposition generate the crisis:

1. **"Forbidden comparisons."** Some constituent 2×2s "compare units treated at two different times, using the later-treated group as a control before its treatment begins and then the earlier-treated group as a control after its treatment begins." Once the earlier-treated group's dynamic effects have arrived, using it as a control subtracts its own treatment path from the contrast.
2. **Variance-driven weights with no economic interpretation.** The weights "are proportional to timing group sizes and the variance of the treatment dummy in each pair, which is highest for units treated in the middle of the panel." For a unit switching on at period k of T, the weight-relevant variance is p(1−p) with p = (T−k+1)/T; this is maximized at p = 1/2 (maximum weight 0.25) and vanishes at the panel edges.
3. **The identifying requirement.** "A causal interpretation of two-way fixed effects DD estimates requires both a parallel trends assumption and treatment effects that are constant over time." Negative weights arise when average effects vary over time, so the TWFE coefficient can be negative even when every cohort-time effect is positive; Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe (2023; https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf) give the canonical example in which Medicaid expansion effects on coverage are positive and growing over time yet β_post is negative.

Parallel results from de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (*AER* 110(9): 2964–2996, 2020; https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20181169) showed the TWFE coefficient is a weighted sum of group-period ATEs "with weights that may be negative," so it "may for instance be negative while all of the ATEs are positive"—and in their two revisited applications, roughly half the weights were negative. Sun and Abraham (2021) added the event-study version: leads and lags in a TWFE event-study regression are contaminated by effects from other relative periods, so "apparent pretrends can arise solely from treatment effects heterogeneity" (https://lsun20.github.io/event_studies_paper.pdf).

The exposure was enormous. De Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille's survey (*Econometrics Journal* 26(3), 2023; https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w29691/w29691.pdf) found that **26 of the 100 most-cited papers published in the AER from 2015 to 2019 estimate at least one TWFE regression**; their AER paper separately reported that **20% of all empirical AER articles between 2010 and 2012** used a TWFE regression to estimate treatment effects. Baker, Larcker and Wang (*JFE* 144(2): 370–395, 2022; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X22000204) counted 751 DiD papers in top finance (439) and accounting (312) journals, 2000–2019, of which 366/751 = **48.9% used staggered designs** (with 394/407 ≈ 96.8% of published staggered papers appearing since 2010); re-examining published results with alternative estimators, they found estimates that "differ substantially from prior papers." Currie, Kleven and Zwiers (2020) document that almost 25% of NBER applied-micro working papers reference DiD (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w26715/w26715.pdf), and Goldsmith-Pinkham's credibility-revolution audit (NBER WP 35051; https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w35051/w35051.pdf) reports that as of 2024, 63% of applied-micro papers mention experimental or quasi-experimental methods, with growth driven overwhelmingly by DiD. Feng, Wang and Zhou (https://personal.ntu.edu.sg/qfeng/Top%2027_20260313_FengWangZhou.pdf) estimate DiD at roughly 25% of microdata identification across 27 top journals in 2014–2018, rising to ~30% in the AER. Athey and Imbens (*JoE* 2022; https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/econom/v226y2022i1p62-79.html) added a design-based qualification: under *randomly assigned* adoption dates, standard DiD is unbiased for a particular weighted average effect—but timing is rarely random in practice.

## 2. The Three Families of Solutions

All three remedies share one architectural core, well summarized by Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe (RSBP, *JoE* 235: 2218–2244, 2023; https://psantanna.com/files/RSBP_DiD_Review.pdf): **isolate clean 2×2 (or untreated-observation) comparisons and aggregate them with researcher-chosen, policy-relevant weights**. They differ in the comparison group, the base period, the estimation platform, the strength of the parallel-trends assumption, inference, and efficiency. Notably, all three canonical papers—Goodman-Bacon, Sun–Abraham, and Callaway–Sant'Anna—appeared in the *same issue*, *Journal of Econometrics* 225(2), December 2021, a structural marker of the field's consolidation.

### 2.1 Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021): Two-Stage Group-Time ATT Aggregation

(*JoE* 225(2): 200–230; https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020.pdf)

CS define the building-block estimand **ATT(g,t) = E[Y_t(g) − Y_t(0) | G_g = 1]**—the average effect at calendar time t for the cohort first treated at g—and proceed in a deliberately modular identification → aggregation → inference architecture:

- **Stage 1 (identification/estimation):** Each ATT(g,t) is estimated as a long difference from the cohort's last pre-treatment period (base period g−1) against a clean comparison group—**never-treated or not-yet-treated** units—via outcome regression, inverse probability weighting, or a **doubly robust** (DR/AIPW) combination. Parallel trends may hold **conditionally on covariates**, a defining feature none of the other main estimators matched at the outset.
- **Stage 2 (aggregation):** The researcher aggregates ATT(g,t) with explicit weights into an overall ATT, cohort-specific averages, calendar-time averages, or an event-study path over relative time e = t − g.
- **Inference:** A multiplier bootstrap delivers **simultaneous (uniform) confidence bands** across the whole event-study path, rather than pointwise intervals (https://bcallaway11.github.io/did/articles/did-basics.html).
- **Anticipation:** Handled through an explicit `anticipation` parameter that quarantines k pre-treatment periods from the base period.

Heterogeneity is the estimand, not a nuisance: unrestricted variation across g and t is permitted. The empirical illustration is minimum-wage effects on teen employment, 2001–2007. Software: R `did`, Stata `csdid`, Python ports.

### 2.2 Sun and Abraham (2021): The Interaction-Weighted Estimator

(*JoE* 225(2): 175–199; https://lsun20.github.io/event_studies_paper.pdf)

SA proceed in two steps. First, a diagnostic decomposition: in the standard event-study TWFE regression, each lead/lag coefficient μ_ℓ is a **non-convex weighted average of cohort-specific effects CATT(e,ℓ) from its own and other relative periods**, with weights recoverable from an auxiliary regression on cohort shares (implemented in `eventstudyweights`). This is the precise sense in which heterogeneity fabricates spurious pre-trends. Second, the fix: run a **fully saturated regression with cohort × relative-time interactions**,

Y_{i,t} = α_i + λ_t + Σ_g Σ_e δ_{g,e}·1{G_i = g}·D^e_{i,t} + ε_{i,t},

then re-aggregate the estimated CATT(e,ℓ) using sample cohort shares ν_ℓ = Σ_e CATT(e,ℓ)·Pr{E_i = e | E_i ∈ [ℓ, T̄]}—i.e., weighting each cohort by the share of units actually observed at that relative period. The comparison group is **never-treated or last-treated** cohorts; inference is pointwise. Implementation: Stata `eventstudyinteract` (https://github.com/lsun20/eventstudyinteract) or `fixest::feols(y ~ sunab(cohort, time) | unit + time)` in R.

Two clarifications matter for practice. Sant'Anna's own slides note that the SA estimator **coincides numerically with CS when there are no covariates and the never-treated/last-treated cohort is used as the comparison group** (https://psantanna.com/files/SBE1.pdf)—SA is best understood as the event-study-focused, regression-native cousin of CS rather than a fundamentally different identification strategy. And SA's consistency result (their Proposition 4) maintains a no-anticipation assumption.

### 2.3 Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024): The Imputation Estimator

(*Review of Economic Studies* 91(6): 3253–3285; https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419; published version http://eprints.lse.ac.uk/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf)

BJS take a philosophically different route. Rather than constructing group-time 2×2 cells:

1. **Fit the untreated outcome model**—unit fixed effects α̂_i and time fixed effects β̂_t—using **only untreated observations** (never-treated plus pre-treatment observations of eventually-treated units);
2. **Impute counterfactuals** Ŷ_it(0) = α̂_i + β̂_t for every treated observation and compute τ̂_it = Y_it − α̂_i − β̂_t;
3. **Aggregate** with researcher-chosen weights into event-time effects, overall ATTs, calendar-time averages, or arbitrary policy targets.

Because *all* untreated observations inform the counterfactual (rather than a single g−1 base period per cohort), BJS prove the estimator is **semiparametrically efficient** under unrestricted treatment-effect heterogeneity—the source of its precision advantage: confidence intervals roughly **50% shorter than Callaway–Sant'Anna's and 2–3.5× shorter than Sun–Abraham's** in simulations and applications where effects are plausibly homogeneous (https://diff-diff.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/imputation.html; https://www.causalreview.com/articles/the-borusyak-jaravel-spiess-imputation-estimator-efficient-did-for-staggered-adoption-settings). The framework extends to time-varying controls, triple-difference designs, and some non-binary treatments, and develops formal tests of the identifying assumptions. Their tax-rebate application finds a notional first-quarter MPC of 8–11%—about half the benchmark used to calibrate macro models. Software: Stata `did_imputation`, `event_plot`.

**The Gardner/Wooldridge equivalence.** Gardner's two-stage estimator (`did2s`; Butts & Gardner, *R Journal* 2022, https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2022-048/) and Wooldridge's (2021) extended TWFE regression are the regression cousins of imputation: stage one estimates the unit/time structure on untreated observations; stage two regresses adjusted outcomes on treatment indicators. A Boston University working paper (https://www.bu.edu/econ/files/2024/07/two-stage-differences-in-differences.pdf) reports that its two-stage procedure provides "**identical point estimates**" to BJS "with different variance estimators," and—simulating randomly drawn state minimum-wage laws on a 42-year panel extending Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan—claims the best rejection-rate/speed/efficiency performance among CS, SA, Wooldridge, BJS, and de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille. Its most sobering finding: "even in cases with homogeneous treatment effects… **other heterogeneity-robust estimators tend to yield much larger standard errors**" than TWFE—the practical price of robustness.

### 2.4 The Wider Family

Adjacent members include de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille's `did_multiplegt` (switcher-based Wald-DiD ratios accommodating treatment reversals; *AER* 2020), Cengiz et al.'s (2019) stacked cohort-specific datasets, Wooldridge's two-stage Mundlak regression, and Dube, Girardi, Jordà and Taylor's LP-DiD local-projection approach (NBER WP 31184), which "subsumes many of the recent solutions" under a flexible clean-control condition. Roth and Sant'Anna (*JPE: Microeconomics* 1(4): 669–709, 2023; https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/726581) replace parallel trends with a design-based assumption of (quasi-)random treatment timing and derive the efficient estimator under that assumption—attaining standard-error reductions of 2× or more relative to CS/SA, with confidence intervals up to 8× shorter in their police-training application (https://psantanna.com/files/Roth_SantAnna_Staggered.pdf). This is a stronger identifying assumption than PT, but it clarifies what the efficiency frontier looks like when timing can be defended as random.

## 3. Assumption-by-Assumption Comparison

| Dimension | Callaway–Sant'Anna | Sun–Abraham | BJS / Gardner imputation | TWFE (baseline) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Parallel trends** | Generalized to all (g,t) pairs; may hold **conditionally on covariates** (OR/IPW/DR); researcher chooses never-treated (stronger) or not-yet-treated (weaker) comparison | Unconditional PT relative to never- or last-treated cohorts | PT/additive separability of Y(0) across **all** untreated observations panel-wide—the strongest single form, which buys efficiency | Canonical unconditional PT |
| **TE homogeneity** | None required; heterogeneity across g,t is the estimand | None required; constructed to be free of cross-period contamination | None required for consistency; homogeneity drives the efficiency edge | **Required** (with PT) for causal interpretation |
| **Anticipation** | Explicit `anticipation` horizon; identification written as PT for t ≥ g−δ | No anticipation maintained (Prop. 4); handled by binning/excluding leads | No anticipation in the canonical event-study assumptions; addressed via lead exclusion and formal assumption tests | Contaminates leads and lags without acknowledgment |
| **Comparison group** | Never-treated or not-yet-treated | Never-treated or last-treated | All untreated observations pooled | Everyone, including already-treated units |
| **Base period** | Single last pre-treatment period (g−1) per cohort | Omitted relative period −1 (per cohort) | Global: all pre-treatment periods | Implicit, all periods |
| **Inference** | Multiplier bootstrap, **simultaneous** bands | Pointwise CIs (bootstrap possible) | Asymptotic; clustered/residual bootstrap; built-in pre-trend tests | Conventional |
| **Efficiency** | Lowest of the three robust options (single base period) | Intermediate | Highest under correct specification; ~50% shorter CIs than CS | Smallest SEs but biased target |
| **Generality** | Panel and repeated cross-sections; flexible covariates | Panel; covariates via interactions | Time-varying controls, triple-diff, some non-binary treatments | Panel |

Three contrasts deserve emphasis.

**Parallel trends: strength vs. conditioning.** CS make the weakest demands in one dimension—PT can fail unconditionally and hold only conditional on X—and give the researcher an explicit lever (never-treated vs. not-yet-treated) that trades assumption strength against sample size. BJS require the untreated-observations model to hold across the *whole* panel, which is what allows borrowing strength from every clean observation. Marcus and Sant'Anna (*JAERE*; https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/711509) formalize this as an explicit "robustness vs. efficiency trade-off in terms of the strength of the underlying PTA," arguing practitioners should state which PTA version identifies which parameter. Chiu, Lan, Liu and Xu (2023/2025, *American Political Science Review*) similarly partition the literature into "DID extensions" built from local 2×2s (CS, SA) versus "imputation methods" that "embed DID's functional form assumptions in their outcome models" (BJS, Gardner, Wooldridge).

**Homogeneity plays no identifying role—but a large efficiency role.** All three families are consistent under unrestricted heterogeneity; homogeneity only determines whether imputation's efficiency advantage (and TWFE's even smaller standard errors) is realized. The diff-diff tutorial's practical rule: "if all three [CS, SA, BJS] agree, results are robust; if they disagree, investigate heterogeneity" (https://diff-diff.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/11_imputation_did.html).

**Anticipation is a shared maintained assumption with different handling.** CS make the anticipation horizon an explicit design parameter (discard k pre-periods, sacrifice information, gain cleanliness); SA require no anticipation for consistency and handle it by binning or excluding leads; BJS exclude leads and supply estimator-consistent tests. RSBP (2023, §3.4) flag that no-anticipation is often *implicitly* violated under staggered adoption—an event-study plot with systematically negative leads is consistent with anticipation rather than pre-trends.

## 4. Methodological Dominance in AER/QJE/JPE Labor and Health Economics, 2020–2024

**A necessary caveat first.** No published, systematic estimator-by-estimator adoption audit exists for AER/QJE/JPE labor- and health-economics papers specifically in 2020–2024. Roth's (2022) calibration survey covers 2014–2018 (pre-adoption); Baker–Larcker–Wang (2022) audit finance and accounting; Chiu et al. audit political science. The conclusions below are triangulated from citation counts, software ecosystems, synthesis literature, and field-specific guides—and the *direction* of the conclusion is high-confidence while the *magnitudes* are not measured.

**The triangulating evidence:**

- **Synthesis emphasis.** In RSBP's definitive practitioner-facing review, Callaway–Sant'Anna receives 21 mentions across 4 sections, versus Sun–Abraham 11/3, de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille 7, BJS 5, and Goodman-Bacon 4 (https://econbase.org/papers/2201.01194.html). CS is discussed roughly twice as often as SA and four times as often as BJS.
- **Citation and software scale.** Scott Cunningham's package audit (https://www.scunning.com/files/package_audit_r4.pdf) reports CS (2021) at **10,750 citations in six years** with **six independent software implementations** (R `did`, R `ddml`, Stata `csdid`, Stata `csdid2`, Python `differences`, Python `diff-diff`; R `did` at 383 GitHub stars), noting "at this adoption scale, implementation differences affect thousands of applied papers." (Goodman-Bacon shows ~2,209 RePEc citations—not directly comparable, since RePEc undercounts relative to Google Scholar.) By contrast, the `did_imputation` package had only ~29 citations as of 2024—a different object (package-level vs. method-level), but consistent with BJS's later diffusion, since the *RES* publication (91(6), 2024) postdates most of the window and its 2020–2024 footprint was largely in working-paper form.
- **The wrapper-package norm.** The Stata ecosystem now ships `csdid`, `did_imputation`, `eventstudyinteract`, `did_multiplegt`, `did2s`, `stackedev`, `jwdid`, and `xtevent` alongside native `xtdidregress`/`hdidregress` (Stata Journal 2024; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1536867X241297914), and `did2s`'s `event_study` wrapper runs *every* modern estimator under one syntax "allowing quick estimation and plotting of every alternative event study estimator." The existence of meta-packages built to run all estimators side-by-side is itself the clearest marker that **report-multiple-estimators**, not winner-take-all, became the applied norm.
- **Health economics.** The *Annual Review of Public Health* guide "Designing Difference-in-Difference Studies with Staggered Adoption" (2024; https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-publhealth-061022-050825) builds its checklist around the Goodman-Bacon decomposition and the new estimators while noting "no practical guide exists for addressing these new critiques in public health research"—evidence that health-economics adoption was still consolidating. An epidemiology primer lists heterogeneity-robust estimators with **Callaway and Sant'Anna first** as "increasingly being implemented by epidemiologists" (https://escholarship.org/content/qt0029j9f8/qt0029j9f8.pdf). Margolis et al. (2023, *Epidemiology*; https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001611) compared TWFE, group-time ATT, cohort ATT, and target-trial approaches for Medicaid expansion effects on preterm birth: TWFE estimated expansion *increased* preterm birth risk (RD: 0.12, 95% CI: 0.02, 0.22) while group-time ATT, cohort ATT, and target-trial approaches estimated protective or null effects; their simulations confirmed TWFE "performed well when treatment effects were constant and less well under heterogeneous and dynamic effects."
- **Adjacent-field replication.** Chiu, Lan, Liu and Xu surveyed 102 articles (2017–2023) in three leading political science journals, finding most still used TWFE, but among adopters of HTE-robust estimators **Callaway–Sant'Anna was the most commonly adopted**, followed by imputation and then Sun–Abraham; they also found "HTE-robust estimators yield qualitatively similar but highly variable results" and that "many studies are underpowered when accounting for HTE and potential PT violations."

**The dominance verdict.** On this evidence:

1. **Callaway–Sant'Anna is the modal default** heterogeneity-robust estimator—the strongest claim to "dominance" among the new methods—anchored by the `did`/`csdid` ecosystem, first-party multi-language maintenance, doubly robust covariate handling (especially valuable in health applications with covariate-heavy claims data and repeated cross sections), and validated simultaneous inference. Labor applications include sick-pay mandates (Pichler and Wen), noncompete agreements, and the Better Work program (*Economics Letters* 228, 2023).
2. **Sun–Abraham is the standard event-study companion**, especially in labor economics where the event-study plot is the native genre and `fixest`'s `sunab()` integration minimizes implementation friction; health-economics event studies routinely cite "Sun and Abraham (2021); Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021)" jointly.
3. **Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess is ascendant but lags within the window**—its *RES* publication in 2024 means its 2020–2024 influence ran through the 2021 working paper; it is the efficiency-oriented choice where homogeneity is plausible (e.g., the Clemens et al. minimum-wage pre-analysis plan selecting `did_imputation` for its "attractive properties for our setting").
4. **Dominance is not exclusive, and the transition is incomplete.** The dominant *practice* in top journals by 2023–2024 is reporting a heterogeneity-robust estimator (most often CS) alongside TWFE or SA, plus sensitivity analysis—not the wholesale replacement of TWFE, which persists as a transitional specification in 2020–2022 papers, often with a Goodman-Bacon diagnostic. Adoption of robust estimators in labor and health at the very top journals remained partial through the window.

**How authors justify the choice.** Applied authors overwhelmingly do **not** run their own Monte Carlo simulations to select among estimators. Justification typically consists of (a) citing the critique and the original methodological papers for theoretical guarantees, (b) following RSBP's checklist, and (c) reporting multiple estimators side-by-side as robustness. Monte Carlo evidence is supplied *by the methods papers themselves* (BJS's simulations; the BU two-stage state-law simulations; Gardner's Monte Carlo evidence) and by field-specific simulation studies (Margolis et al. 2023; Baker–Larcker–Wang 2022, whose re-examinations "differ substantially from prior papers"), not by applied papers. Formal sensitivity analysis via Rambachan–Roth's `HonestDiD` appears in a growing minority of papers after 2023. This gap between the severity of the diagnostics and the thinness of applied justification is precisely what motivated the RSBP synthesis; a systematic text-mining audit of AER/QJE/JPE in the spirit of Currie–Kleven–Zwiers remains the missing piece of evidence.

## 5. How the New Estimators Address Roth's (2022) Pre-Trends Concerns

Roth, "Pretest with Caution" (*AER: Insights* 4(3): 305–322, 2022; https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aeri.20210236), calibrating simulations to his survey of **70 papers in three leading journals (2014–2018)** displaying event-study plots, documents two failures of conventional pre-trend testing:

1. **Low power.** Linear pre-trend violations against which conventional tests had only ~50% power would produce bias of magnitude *similar to the estimated treatment effect itself*. A non-significant pre-test is close to uninformative.
2. **Pre-test bias from conditioning.** Draws that "survive" a pre-test are a selected sample: conditional on passing, conventional 95% confidence intervals failed to include the true average post-treatment effect roughly **half the time in the median paper**, and conditional bias could exceed **twice** the unconditional bias.

The new estimators respond through four complementary mechanisms:

**(a) Eliminating contamination-driven spurious pre-trends (Sun–Abraham).** Because under TWFE "apparent pretrends can arise solely from treatment effects heterogeneity," a TWFE pre-test is not merely low-powered—it can be affirmatively misleading, since large post-treatment effects in early cohorts contaminate estimated leads for later cohorts. The IW estimator is free of this contamination, so its pre-period coefficients are interpretable as genuine pre-trends; the `eventstudyweights` decomposition lets authors quantify how much heterogeneity would be needed to fabricate a given apparent pre-trend. CS and BJS achieve the same decontamination by construction, making pre-period coefficients estimand-consistent so that pretests at least test the right object.

**(b) Power-aware and equivalence-based pretesting.** RSBP's checklist explicitly recommends "diagnostics of the power of the pre-test against relevant alternatives and/or non-inferiority tests" alongside the event-study plot. Roth's `pretrends` R package (https://github.com/jonathandroth/pretrends) computes the minimum detectable violation for a given power level—reframing the pretest from a binary "no significant lead" ritual into a statement about what violations the test *could* have detected. A pretest powered only against implausibly large violations is revealed as uninformative.

**(c) Separation of estimation and testing (BJS).** Because the imputation model is fit entirely on untreated observations, BJS's pre-trend assessment (comparing imputed versus actual pre-treatment outcomes; formal tests developed in the paper) is structurally independent of the treatment-effect estimates. As the paper states, "this approach avoids the contamination of the tests by treatment-effect heterogeneity shown by Sun and Abraham (2021). Moreover, our strategy circumvents the inference problems after pre-testing that were pointed out by Roth (2022), **under spherical errors**." The spherical-errors qualification is important: the clean circumvention of pre-test bias holds under spherical errors; outside that case the separation helps but the guarantee is qualified. This is nonetheless the most direct architectural answer to Roth's conditioning critique among the estimator families.

**(d) Sensitivity analysis replacing binary pretesting (Rambachan–Roth 2023).** "A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends" (*RES* 90(5): 2555–2591; https://www.restud.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/MS30764manuscript.pdf) replaces exact parallel trends with **restrictions on how large post-treatment violations can be relative to pre-treatment differences in trends**: smoothness restrictions (Δ^SD, bounding period-to-period changes in the violation) and relative-magnitude restrictions (Δ^RM, bounding the post-treatment violation at M̄ times the maximal pre-treatment violation). The parameter is partially identified with **uniformly valid** confidence intervals, implemented in `HonestDiD` (R/Stata). Authors can report a breakdown value—how large a violation would overturn the conclusion—instead of a pass/fail test. The toolkit is explicitly designed to compose with the new estimators: Sant'Anna's `CS_RR` repository links `did` with `HonestDiD`.

**The emergent consensus workflow.** The de facto best-practice stack in labor and health applications by 2023–2024 is: (i) TWFE alongside a heterogeneity-robust estimator (usually CS); (ii) a joint Wald pre-trend test across all pre-treatment group-time cells (the `did` package's multiplicity-adjusted test); (iii) an SA interaction-weighted event study as robustness; (iv) power diagnostics via `pretrends`; and (v) an HonestDiD M̄ breakdown analysis. In this stack the estimators fix *contamination* (what the pretest measures), the power diagnostics fix *informativeness* (what the pretest could detect), and HonestDiD fixes the *conditioning* problem (inference no longer filtered through a pass/fail pretest).

## 6. Bottom Line

**Common core, different mechanics.** CS (group-time ATTs from a g−1 base period, aggregated with user weights), SA (saturated cohort × relative-time interactions reweighted by cohort shares), and BJS/Gardner (untreated-observations imputation) all eliminate forbidden comparisons and negative weights by construction and are consistent under unrestricted treatment-effect heterogeneity. They differ along measurable axes: comparison group (not-yet-treated vs. never/last-treated vs. all untreated), base period (single g−1 vs. the global pre-treatment panel), parallel-trends flexibility (CS uniquely supports conditional PT with doubly robust estimation; BJS impose the strongest global form and are repaid with semiparametric efficiency), inference (simultaneous bootstrap bands vs. pointwise), and precision (BJS ~50% shorter CIs than CS under homogeneity; robust estimators generally yield larger SEs than TWFE even under homogeneity).

**Assumptions.** Homogeneity has exited the identifying assumptions entirely and survives only as an efficiency consideration; no-anticipation is a shared maintained assumption with estimator-specific handling; the real action is in the *strength and conditioning* of the parallel-trends assumption and the explicit robustness–efficiency trade-off (Marcus–Sant'Anna) that the comparison-group and base-period choices encode.

**Dominance.** On triangulated bibliometric, software, and synthesis evidence—but absent a systematic AER/QJE/JPE labor/health audit—**Callaway–Sant'Anna achieved de facto dominance as the default heterogeneity-robust estimator by 2024**, with Sun–Abraham the standard event-study companion and BJS the ascendant efficiency-oriented alternative whose main influence within the window ran through working-paper form. Dominance is plural rather than exclusive: the dominant *practice* is multi-estimator reporting plus sensitivity analysis, adoption remains incomplete, and Monte Carlo justification by applied authors is rare—authors lean on the methods papers' simulations, the RSBP checklist, and Rambachan–Roth sensitivity bounds instead.

**Roth (2022).** The new estimators address the pre-trends critique indirectly but substantively: SA (and by construction CS and BJS) remove heterogeneity-driven spurious pre-trends so pretests test the right object; power-aware diagnostics (`pretrends`, non-inferiority testing) address low power; BJS's estimation/testing separation circumvents pre-test bias (under spherical errors); and HonestDiD's partial-identification sensitivity analysis replaces the binary pretesting logic Roth critiqued. The combined package—robust estimator + power diagnostics + M̄ breakdown reporting—is the current best-practice answer, and its rapid codification in checklists, guides, and software suggests Roth's critique has already reshaped the evidentiary standard in the journals where the debate began.

# Acadia Realty Trust (NYSE: AKR): Capital Allocation, Risk Management, and the Economics of Portfolio Transformation

## Executive Summary

The evidence supports a verdict of **effective capital allocation with a deliberate, measurable cost of transition**. Acadia's Q1 2024 segment economics confirm a structurally higher-quality Core Portfolio (32.4% operating margin vs. 17.0% for the Funds segment), which is precisely the business toward which management is steering capital. The January 2025 Renaissance Portfolio acquisition converted a passive 20% equity-method stake into a 68% controlling, consolidated interest in a premier Georgetown street-retail asset — a textbook execution of the stated "controlling interests" strategy, at a net equity cost of roughly $43 million attributable to the acquired 48% stake. The 2025 impairment cluster — $37.2 million consolidated across Fund III and Fund IV, plus a $3.5 million mark on the unconsolidated Bald Hill Road joint venture — was triggered in 100% of consolidated cases by a *reduced holding period*, marking these as exit-timing decisions rather than operating failures; Acadia's own net burden was only ~$8.9 million (24% of gross), with limited partners absorbing the rest. Finally, the ~$315–325 million increase in consolidated debt during 2025 was equity-supported (~$277.5 million of ATM forward settlements) and accretively structured (a $250 million term loan at ~4.6% all-in), and pro-rata leverage *improved* from the mid-6x range to 4.9x–5.6x depending on the EBITDA measure. The borrowing strategy therefore reads as value-creating rather than constrained, and the overall pattern signals genuine — though not yet fully proven — management confidence in the dual-platform transformation.

---

## 1. Baseline Business Quality: Q1 2024 Operating Margins by Segment

The Q1 2024 10-Q segment disclosure (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017024050536/R92.htm) provides the cleanest pre-transformation baseline for the two-platform model.

**Core Portfolio (three months ended March 31, 2024):**
- Total revenues: $53,538K
- Property operating expenses and real estate taxes: $(17,919)K
- Depreciation and amortization: $(18,267)K
- **Operating income: $17,352K**

**Opportunity Funds (three months ended March 31, 2024):**
- Total revenues: $37,818K
- Property operating expenses and real estate taxes: $(13,523)K
- Depreciation and amortization: $(16,673)K
- Loss related to a previously disposed property: $(1,198)K
- **Operating income: $6,424K**

**Calculated margins:**

| Metric | Core Portfolio | Opportunity Funds |
|---|---|---|
| Operating margin (Op. income ÷ revenue) | $17,352 / $53,538 = **32.4%** | $6,424 / $37,818 = **17.0%** |
| NOI-type margin ((Rev − PropOpEx) ÷ Rev) | $35,619 / $53,538 = **66.5%** | $24,295 / $37,818 = **64.2%** |
| D&A intensity (D&A ÷ revenue) | **34.1%** | **44.1%** |

Three findings matter for business quality:

1. **The Core operating margin is ~1.9x the Funds' margin — a 15.4 percentage-point gap — and the gap is not generated at the property level.** Property-level NOI margins are nearly identical (66.5% vs. 64.2%). The entire divergence comes from below the NOI line: the Funds carry far heavier depreciation relative to revenue (44.1% vs. 34.1%) and absorb disposition-related noise such as the $1.2 million Q1 2024 loss on a previously disposed property. This is a structural feature of the value-add/opportunistic model — shorter holds, intensive repositioning, and frequent recycling — not an operating deficiency, but it means the Funds segment's *accounting* earnings quality is inherently lower and more volatile than the Core's. The same volatility is visible on the upside: the Funds segment recorded a $24,995K realized/unrealized gain in Q1 2023, showing that fund returns are realized episodically through disposition rather than smoothly through operations.

2. **The quality gap is widening, not closing.** Per the Q1 2024 10-Q segment reporting (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017024050536/R38.htm), in Q1 2023 Core earned a 30.2% operating margin and Funds 21.9% — an 8.3-point differential. By Q1 2024 the gap had expanded to 15.4 points. Core revenues grew 7.5% year-over-year while Funds revenues grew 18%, yet Funds operating income actually *declined* from $7.0 million to $6.4 million — incremental fund revenue produced negative marginal profit. City Point (Fund II) alone represented $553.4 million of the Funds segment's $1.6 billion in total assets, illustrating the capital intensity embedded in that platform.

3. **The Core's earnings engine was already compounding.** Same-store NOI grew 5.7% in Q1 2024, the twelfth consecutive quarter above 5% — the cash-flow durability that justifies consolidating more assets into this segment.

**Baseline conclusion:** The Core Portfolio is the structurally superior earnings stream — efficient conversion of NOI to operating profit, durable same-store growth, and lower earnings volatility. The Funds platform is a value-creation engine whose returns arrive in lumpy, disposition-driven form with a heavy D&A drag. This baseline is the analytical foundation for everything that follows: management's strategic moves in 2024–2025 systematically shift capital, control, and debt capacity toward the higher-margin Core/REIT side of the house.

---

## 2. The Renaissance Portfolio Acquisition: Net Cash Investment and the Controlling-Interest Thesis

### Transaction economics

On **January 23, 2025**, Acadia acquired an additional **48% economic interest** in the Renaissance Portfolio — the Georgetown Renaissance Collection in Washington, D.C., comprising 36 retail stores along M Street, spanning over 318,000 square feet across 20 buildings in one of the nation's premier street-retail corridors — for a **purchase price of $117.9 million in cash**, raising its stake from 20% to **68%** and obtaining a controlling financial interest for the first time (FY2025 10-K, Note 2: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526051677/R16.htm; Q3 2025 10-Q Note 2: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312525256341/R48.htm).

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Gross portfolio fair value | $245.7M |
| Existing mortgage debt (remains in venture) | $156.1M |
| Implied underlying equity value ($245.7M − $156.1M) | **$89.6M** |
| Purchase price for 48% stake (cash) | **$117.9M** |
| Portfolio-level LTV at acquisition | 63.5% |
| Loss on change in control (remeasurement of prior 20%) | **$9.6M** |

### The net cash investment calculation

The $117.9 million headline price is best understood as a **gross-asset-value payment**: 48% × $245.7M = $117.9M. Because the $156.1 million of mortgage debt stays inside the venture and attaches proportionally to the acquired interest, the net *equity* outlay is:

- 48% × $156.1M of venture debt = $74.9M
- $117.9M cash − $74.9M debt attaching to the acquired interest = **$43.0M of net equity** — exactly 48% of the implied $89.6M equity value

In other words, the pricing was economically clean: Acadia paid precisely pro-rata for the underlying equity once the assumed debt is netted, with no visible control premium in the unit price. Acadia's resulting 68% interest in the underlying equity equates to roughly **$60.9 million** (68% × $89.6M). The transaction consolidated the full $245.7M asset base and $156.1M of debt onto Acadia's balance sheet, with a 32% noncontrolling interest carve-out for the EastBanc partner. Against this, Acadia recognized a **$9.6 million non-cash loss on change in control** from remeasuring its pre-existing 20% equity-method interest to fair value — a candid admission that the prior carrying mark exceeded fair value, and a real, if non-cash, cost of stepping up to control. Prior to the deal, that 20% stake generated only equity-method earnings of $2.1M in Q1 2024 (per the segment disclosure above); consolidation now brings the portfolio's NOI into the segment with the 32.4% operating margin rather than the 17.0% fund segment.

### Post-closing balance-sheet optimization

On **January 24, 2025 — one day after closing** — the venture modified the assumed property mortgage, originally SOFR + 2.65% maturing November 6, 2026, down to **SOFR + 1.55%**, a ~110 basis-point reduction. The rate cut was achieved through a principal paydown funded by Acadia as a **note receivable from the venture bearing interest at 9.11%**, maturing November 2026 and eliminated in consolidation (10-K Note 2/Note 7, ibid.).

On the paydown's dollar quantum, the panels report the same transaction with minor variance: two panel analyses tied to the 10-K cite a **$50.0 million** Acadia-funded principal paydown (implying roughly $550K of annual interest savings on that tranche at 110 bps), while a third describes a **$54.1 million** paydown funded via a **$57.1 million** note receivable, the ~$3.0 million difference representing capitalized costs (Q2 2025 10-Q: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025100264/akr-20250630.htm). One analysis additionally notes a subsequent **$57.1 million** paydown during 2025 representing the 32% noncontrolling interest holders' share of the total payment. The rate reduction itself — SOFR + 2.65% to SOFR + 1.55% — is corroborated across all three accounts and is the economically material fact; the precise paydown quantum should be read as approximately $50–57 million depending on whether capitalized costs and the NCI share are included.

### Strategic alignment assessment

The acquisition aligns with the controlling-interest strategy on three dimensions:

1. **Control and consolidation.** Moving 20% → 68% converts a passive, fee-adjacent equity-method position into direct control over leasing, operations, and capital decisions on a trophy D.C. asset, and shifts its earnings into the higher-quality Core/REIT segment.
2. **Cost-of-capital arbitrage at the asset level.** With SOFR near 4.3% in early 2025, the pre-modification mortgage ran at roughly 7.0% all-in; the paydown cut the external spread by 110 bps. Because the 9.11% intercompany note is eliminated in consolidation, its rate is an internal transfer price, not a consolidated interest cost — the economic substance is that Acadia injected ~$50 million of corporate equity to delever the venture and cheapen its third-party debt, capturing 68% of the resulting NOI uplift.
3. **Disciplined pricing.** Payment at exactly pro-rata gross asset value, with the seller retaining a 32% minority stake, avoided a control premium while still delivering governance control.

**Caveats.** The $9.6 million change-in-control loss signals prior marks were optimistic. And one panel reads the 9.11% intercompany note as a hint of *asset-level capital constraint* — had the venture been readily financeable at market, external refinancing might have been preferable to committing corporate capital at a double-digit internal yield. On balance, the deliberate-structure reading is better supported: Acadia simultaneously demonstrated strong market access (a $250M term loan at SOFR + 120 bps, an active ATM forward equity program, and a $1.5B accordion), so the choice to fund the paydown internally looks like balance-sheet retention and spread capture rather than necessity. But the commitment of ~$50 million of corporate liquidity at the asset level is a real use of capital, and it foreshadows the debt discussion in Section 4.

---

## 3. Impairment Charges: Concentration, Timing, and the Shortened-Hold-Period Signal

### The record, 2023–2025

The impairment profile escalated sharply in 2025, and every consolidated fund impairment carried the identical trigger: a **reduced/shortened holding period** (FY2025 10-K, Note 8 — nonrecurring fair value measurements: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526051677/R85.htm).

**2023 (baseline, modest):**
- $3,686K total — one Fund IV property, 146 Geary Street, San Francisco; trigger: reduced holding period.

**2024 (modest, year-end):** $1,678K total (FY2024 10-K fair value disclosures: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025021145/R84.htm):

| Property | Segment | Trigger | Date | Total | Acadia Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1964 Union Street, San Francisco | Fund IV | Reduced holding period | Dec 31, 2024 | $1.17M | $0.24M |
| Mark Plaza, Edwardsville, PA | Core | Reduced projected NOI | Dec 31, 2024 | $0.51M | $0.51M |
| **Total 2024** | | | | **$1.68M** | **$0.75M** |

The Mark Plaza mark is worth flagging: it demonstrates that even Core assets can incur impairments, though the trigger there (reduced projected NOI) differs from the fund-exit trigger and the amount is immaterial.

**2025 (massive escalation, mid-year concentration):**

| Property | Fund | Location | Trigger | Measurement Date | Gross Charge | Acadia Share | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 640 Broadway | Fund III | New York, NY | Reduced holding period | Jun 30, 2025 | $7,240K | $1,777K | Sold Q3 2025 for $49.5M |
| 1035 Third Avenue | Fund IV | New York, NY | Reduced holding period | Jun 30, 2025 | $17,400K | $3,991K | Sold October 2025 for $22.0M |
| Broad Hollow Commons | Fund III | East Farmingdale, NY | Reduced holding period | Sep 30, 2025 | $12,570K | $3,085K | Transferred out of development; FV $21.3M at 10.0% discount / 7.0% cap |
| **Consolidated subtotal** | | | | | **$37,210K** | **$8,853K** | |
| 650 Bald Hill Road | Fund IV (unconsolidated JV) | Warwick, RI | Shortened hold period | 2025 | $3,500K | ~$700K | Sold April 2026 for $20.5M (Acadia share $4.3M) |
| **Grand total 2025** | | | | | **$40,710K** | **~$9,553K** | |

Valuation inputs confirm meaningful rate expansion embedded in the marks: the East Farmingdale valuation used a 10.0% discount rate and 7.0% cap rate; the Fund IV New York property used a 9.25% discount rate and 8.25% cap rate — reflecting both elevated cost of capital and the mid-2025 transaction environment.

### Concentration analysis

- **By trigger:** 100% of consolidated 2025 impairments cite "reduced holding period." This is a *strategic* marker, not an operating one — management elected to monetize faster than the original Fund III/Fund IV business plans contemplated, and accounting requires marking to expected proceeds under the compressed timeline.
- **By timing:** 60.5% of 2025's total impairments were measured at June 30, 2025 and another 30.9% at September 30, 2025 — a six-month window consistent with a single, deliberate portfolio decision rather than scattered deterioration.
- **By geography:** Two New York City properties accounted for $24.6 million (~66% of the consolidated total), plus one Long Island asset (~34%) — a New York metro cluster, raising a legitimate question about whether prior NYC fund valuations were systematically optimistic or whether the market simply moved faster than exit timelines allowed.
- **By fund:** Fund III absorbed $19.8M (48.7%), Fund IV $17.4M (42.7%), and the Bald Hill Road JV $3.5M (8.6%).
- **Year-over-year:** Total impairments surged roughly 24x, from $1.68M in 2024 to $40.7M in 2025.

### Risk absorption and monetization follow-through

Two features materially soften the headline number. First, **the fund structure did its job as a risk-distribution mechanism**: of the $37.2M gross consolidated impairment, Acadia's net share was only **$8.85M (~24%)**; the remaining ~$28.4M was absorbed by fund limited partners and Common OP unitholders. Second, **recognition was rapidly followed by realization**: three of the four impaired assets were monetized within roughly 4–7 months of the charge — 640 Broadway sold in Q3 2025 for $49.5 million, 1035 Third Avenue sold in October 2025 for $22.0 million, and Bald Hill Road sold in April 2026 for $20.5 million (Acadia share $4.3 million; Q1 2026 supplemental: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526321040/akr-ex99_2.htm). This near-immediate conversion of accounting marks into cash proceeds reframes the impairments as *harvesting events* — crystallizing value and recycling capital — rather than write-downs of stranded assets.

### Bald Hill Road: the unconsolidated channel

650 Bald Hill Road in Warwick, RI is a Fund IV unconsolidated joint venture (Acadia interest: 20.81%, per the FY2025 10-K MD&A: https://ebs.publicnow.com/view/EE8EDFEA11ACAA12918AE30A54605A03578B9E86). Because it is unconsolidated, its ~$3.5 million impairment flows through **equity in (losses) earnings of unconsolidated affiliates** rather than the consolidated impairment line; the 10-K explicitly attributes the Investment Management segment's $20.3 million year-over-year deterioration in that line to the Bald Hill Road impairment together with the loss on the Eden Square sale. It is the cleanest example of management exiting a non-strategic, non-core position at acceptable economics — taking the mark, selling within months, and redeploying.

### Risk interpretation

The impairment cluster reveals a genuine structural tension in the fund wind-down: Fund III and Fund IV are no longer pursuing new investments (Fund V's investment period closed in August 2023), so remaining positions must be realized on constrained timelines, and when exit pricing under a compressed timeline falls below carrying value, impairment is mechanical. The NYC clustering suggests prior valuations may have been systematically optimistic, and the 24x year-over-year spike is a real cost of the pivot that investors should not dismiss. But the countervailing evidence is strong: the trigger was uniformly strategic (exit timing, not NOI collapse), Acadia's net economic burden was a fraction of gross, monetization followed within months, and the fund platform has demonstrated it can still deliver for LPs — the Fund V recapitalization alone generated an 18% IRR and 1.9x equity multiple for limited partners (2025 Annual Report: https://acadiarealty.com/wp-content/uploads/2025_Annual_Report.pdf). As the annual report frames it: "Over the past several years, we have evolved this platform away from traditional single closed end funds toward a more flexible multi-channel joint venture structure." The impairments are the price of that evolution, recognized promptly rather than deferred.

---

## 4. The 2025 Borrowing Strategy: Term Loan, Renaissance Paydown, and Net Debt Trajectory

### The $250 million delayed-draw term loan (Q2 2025)

Established via the Third Amendment to the Credit Agreement dated May 29, 2025 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025100264/akr-ex10_1.htm; Q2 2025 earnings release: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025099653/akr-ex99_1.htm):

- **$250M delayed-draw term loan, 5-year term** (maturing ~2030)
- $175M drawn at closing; $75M of additional delayed-draw capacity (subsequently drawn)
- Pricing: **SOFR + 120 bps; all-in effective rate ~4.6%** inclusive of interest-rate swaps
- Proceeds repaid revolver borrowings and a secured obligation
- Accordion feature limit increased to **$1.5 billion**

### Consolidated debt trajectory

| Date | Consolidated Debt | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Dec 31, 2023 | ~$1,881M | — |
| Mar 31, 2024 | ~$1,734M | −$147M |
| Dec 31, 2024 | $1,547,947K (gross long-term debt) | −$186M from Mar 2024 |
| Dec 31, 2025 | $1,873,367K gross / $1,862,906K principal | **+$325M gross / ~+$315M principal** |

Two context points matter. First, the 2025 increase **followed a prior deleveraging cycle** — year-end 2024 debt sat ~$333M below year-end 2023 — so the 2025 build is repositioning from a conservative base, not layering onto stress. Second, the increase is fully explained by strategic items: the $250M term loan, consolidation of the Renaissance mortgage (~$102M net of the paydown), and new property-level debt, partially offset by repayments including a $50M property mortgage repayment and $4.5M of scheduled amortization.

### Leverage trajectory — the decisive metric

Per the Q4 2025 supplemental (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526044722/akr-ex99_2.htm):

| Metric (Dec 31, 2025) | Value |
|---|---|
| Consolidated principal debt | $1,862,906K |
| Total pro-rata debt capitalization | $1,494,658K |
| Pro-rata net debt | $1,154,181K |
| Net Debt / EBITDA | 5.6x |
| Net Debt / **Adjusted** EBITDA | **4.9x** |
| Net Debt / Adj. EBITDA excl. realized gains | 5.2x |
| Net Debt + Preferred / Total Market Cap | 27% |

The trajectory shows steady improvement even as gross debt rose:

| Date | Pro-Rata Net Debt / EBITDA |
|---|---|
| Mar 31, 2024 | 6.6x |
| Jun 30, 2024 | 6.3x |
| Mar 31, 2025 | 5.7x |
| Jun 30, 2025 | 5.5x |
| Sep 30, 2025 | 5.0x |
| Dec 31, 2025 | **5.6x (EBITDA basis) / 4.9x (Adjusted EBITDA basis)** |

The two year-end figures are different measures, not a contradiction: 5.6x against EBITDA and 4.9x against Adjusted EBITDA. Either way, leverage fell roughly three-quarters of a turn to a turn-and-a-half from early-2024 levels while the company absorbed a $156M mortgage consolidation and a quarter-billion-dollar term loan.

### The critical offset: equity capital

The debt story cannot be told without the equity story. Through the ATM forward equity program, Acadia settled **11.2 million shares in Q1 2025 for net proceeds of ~$277.5 million**, and as of December 31, 2025 an additional **14.7 million unsettled forward shares** remained, representing **~$295.5 million** of potential future proceeds. Debt rose ~$315–325M, but equity provided ~$278M of countervailing capital — meaning *net* leverage increased only modestly, which is precisely why the ratios improved.

### Liquidity, maturities, and earnings coverage

- **Dry powder:** $525M+ of revolver capacity, ~$295.5M of unsettled forward equity, and ~$45M of cash — well over $800M of available liquidity against an announced pipeline including $445M of year-to-date 2026 acquisitions and the Henderson Avenue redevelopment.
- **Maturity profile:** The term loan extends duration; the company reports no significant REIT Portfolio debt maturities until 202

# Multi-Tasking Machine Selection for Ti-6Al-4V Aerospace Machining — Nuevo León, México

**DMG MORI NLX 2500SY vs. Mazak Integrex i-400S vs. Okuma Multus U4000**

---

## 0. First, Resolve the Utilization Figure: 15,000 Hours Is Not a Single-Machine Number

A calendar year contains 24 × 365 = **8,760 hours**. 15,000 ÷ 8,760 = 1.71, so no single machine can log 15,000 hours regardless of reliability. The requirement must be re-based before any cost model or machine comparison is valid. The plausible interpretations:

| Scenario | Available hr/machine/yr | Machines needed for 15,000 h |
|---|---|---|
| 2 shifts × 8 h × 250 days | 4,000 | 15,000 ÷ 4,000 = 3.75 → **4 machines** |
| 3 shifts × 8 h × 250 days | 6,000 | 15,000 ÷ 6,000 = 2.5 → **3 machines** |
| 24/7 theoretical maximum | 8,760 | 15,000 ÷ 8,760 = 1.71 (impossible as stated) |
| 24/7 at 85% availability | ~7,446 | 15,000 ÷ 7,446 ≈ **2 machines** (best case, lights-out) |

Three realistic readings of the 15,000-hour figure:

1. **Fleet-level demand** — the part family requires 15,000 hours across 2–4 machines. This is the most defensible reading and changes the exercise from "pick one machine" to "pick a platform you can standardize and scale."
2. **Spindle-hours vs. machine-hours** — monitoring systems log hours per spindle; a twin-spindle machine (main + sub, or main + lower turret) logs roughly 2× machine-hours. 15,000 spindle-hours ≈ 2 spindles × 7,500 h ≈ one machine at ~86% of calendar time — achievable only with lights-out automation and excellent service response.
3. **Inflated "machine hours"** — some shops count warm-up, tool-change and idle states, inflating true spindle-on time by 30–50%.

Practical planning figures: **2,000–2,500 spindle-hr/yr per machine** for single-shift budgeting; **4,000–4,500 hr/yr** for two-shift; anything **beyond ~6,000 hr/yr on one machine is "extreme duty"** and accelerates spindle wear dramatically. Note that this makes the DMG MORI "MASTER spindles with 36-month warranty and unlimited spindle hours" ([dmgmori.com](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)) uniquely valuable under high-utilization duty cycles — it directly underwrites the dominant wear risk in a 3-shift interpretation. **Recommendation: restate the requirement as machine-hours/yr per machine (realistically 4,000–6,000), size the fleet at 3–4 machines, and evaluate the platforms below on standardization, per-hour cost, and scalability.**

---

## 1. Spindle Torque and Rigidity for Ti-6Al-4V

⚠️ **Rating conventions differ between builders and are not directly comparable** (25% ED vs. 30-min vs. 20-min vs. 10-min vs. continuous). Figures below are quoted with their stated duty cycles, and the Mazak spindle package in particular must be confirmed line-item in the quotation (see note below).

| Parameter | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY (2nd Gen) | Mazak Integrex i-400S | Okuma Multus U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main spindle speed | 5,000 rpm (10"); 3,000 rpm (12" opt.) — [us.dmgmori.com](https://us.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd) | 3,300 rpm — [machinetoolindex.com](https://www.machinetoolindex.com) | 4,200 rpm std; 3,000 rpm big-bore — [okuma.com](https://www.okuma.com/products/multus-u4000) |
| Main spindle torque | 828–843 Nm (10"); **1,273 Nm (12" opt.)** | **1,400 Nm (25% ED)** ≈ 1,032 ft-lbf ([Törner listing](https://cnc-toerner.de/pt/maschine/mazak-integrex-i-400-s-18/); [machinetools.com](https://www.machinetools.com/en/models/mazak-integrex-i-400s-1500u)); ~800 Nm continuous | 700/477 Nm (30-min/cont) std; **955/657 Nm** (10-min/cont) high-torque/big-bore — [Okuma MULTUS U brochure, Jun 2025](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf) |
| Main spindle power | 26 kW (10") / 36 kW (12") | 30 kW (40 HP, 30-min) / 22 kW cont — [mmsonline.com Integrex i-series brochure](https://www.mmsonline.com/cdn/cms/low_integrex_%20i-series_ea.pdf) | 22/15 kW std (30-min/cont); 32/22 kW big-bore (20-min/cont) |
| Sub-spindle | 6"–10", up to 577 Nm @ 5,000 rpm (Gen 2); Gen 1: 11 kW @ 6,000 rpm | 4,000 rpm, 22–26 kW; **~500 Nm (369 ft-lbs) per brochure / ~800 Nm (590 ft-lbf) per some listings — confirm package** | 4,000–4,200 rpm, 22/15 kW, ~286–420 Nm |
| Milling spindle | BMT60: 86/56 Nm @ 12,000 rpm (std); High-Torque 100 Nm @ 6,000 rpm | Capto C6: **120 Nm**, 22 kW @ 12,000 rpm (20k opt.) | H1 B-axis head: **120/90 Nm (3-min/cont), 25/19 kW @ 12,000 rpm**, Capto C6 |
| Y-axis travel | ±50 mm (Gen 1) / ±60 mm (Gen 2) | ±130 mm (260 mm total) | **±150 mm (300 mm total)** — class-leading, traveling column |
| Machine mass | ~6,400 kg — **a size class smaller** (ø366 mm swing vs ø650–658 mm) | **16,200 kg** | ~14,000 kg class (confirm with Okuma) |
| Guideways | Slideways (box-type) X/Y/Z + 55 mm roller guides, double-anchored ball screws | Linear roller guides, orthogonal bed | Linear roller (X,Y,Z), diagonal-rib bed |

**Generation caution on the NLX:** the 1st-generation NLX 2500SY main spindle was rated ~426 Nm (40% DC); the 2nd Generation delivers 828–843 Nm (10") and 1,273 Nm with the 12" option. Quote the 2nd Generation explicitly — mixing generations is a real quoting risk ([en.dmgmori.com NLX 2500 2nd Gen](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd); [DMG MORI Gen 2 launch, Sep 2025](https://us.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/nws2522-emo-nlx-2500)).

**Mazak brochure ambiguity:** the same Mazak Integrex i-series documentation lists both a 4,000 rpm / 26 kW / 500 Nm (40% ED) table and the 3,300 rpm / 30 kW / 1,400 Nm (25% ED) figures — these are different spindle packages. Specify and confirm which package is quoted.

**Model-status caution:** the Integrex i-400S is flagged as a discontinued model in at least one industry database ([machinetoolindex.com](https://www.machinetoolindex.com)), with the **Integrex i NEO** (MAZATROL SmoothAi) as the current successor. Verify with Mazak Mexico whether the quoted i-400S is a current build, remaining stock, or used inventory; if it is being phased out, evaluate the i NEO instead — this materially affects 10–15-year parts support and control upgrade paths.

**Rigidity evidence for titanium:**
- **DMG MORI**: FEM-analyzed bed, "**30% higher rigidity than previous series**" with 50%-more-rigid ball-screw drives via enlarged bearings, ribbed castings ([be.dmgmori.com, NLX Innovation Days 2016](https://be.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/chicago-innovation-days-2016-nlx-2500sy-700)). Box-type slideways inherently provide superior damping for the low-frequency vibration typical of titanium roughing. Spindle roundness 0.5 µm and 55 mm-wide guides documented on Gen 2 ([nl.dmgmori.com NLX 2500 world premiere](https://nl.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/nws24-14-world-premiere-nlx-2500)).
- **Mazak**: 16.2 t mass and orthogonal bed give the highest static stiffness-to-mass ratio of the three — important for chatter-prone Ti-6Al-4V milling; supported by an extensive Aerospace Center of Excellence heritage ([Mazak aerospace](https://www.mazak.com/jp-en/products/aerospace/)).
- **Okuma**: **diagonal-rib bed castings** giving "**7× the rigidity**" vs. non-ribbed structure; orthogonal 3-axis column feed with roller bearings — engineered specifically for stable 5-axis machining, with "tough cutting in entire Y-axis range" as an explicit design goal ([Okuma MULTUS U brochure](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf)).

**Analysis for titanium:** Ti-6Al-4V roughing runs at 30–60 m/min with high cutting forces and heat trapped at the cut zone (low thermal conductivity) — so **low-speed torque and damping dominate; top rpm is largely irrelevant** (the 12,000 rpm milling spindles matter mostly for finishing and aluminum). The **Mazak i-400S leads on peak main-spindle torque (1,400 Nm) and structural mass** — the best heavy-roughing combination. The **Okuma U4000 has the strongest sustained-class milling spindle (25/19 kW, 120 Nm)** plus the largest Y-travel and a 40-tool ATC (80 optional) — best for mill-heavy prismatic features on turned parts. The **NLX 2500SY is fundamentally a turning-mill in a smaller size class**; its 12" option (1,273 Nm) closes much of the torque gap for chucked shafts and flanges, but its ≤100 Nm BMT milling drive is not the benchmark for complex prismatic titanium milling.

---

## 2. Recommended Tooling — and the Ceramic Limitation

**Ceramics are effectively excluded for Ti-6Al-4V.** The evidence is unambiguous:

> "Silicon carbide whisker reinforced (WG 300 grade) alumina ceramic tools are not suitable for machining titanium alloys, even when using other cutting environments, due to the accelerated tool wear and chipping/fracture of the cutting edge associated with chemical interactions between the ceramic tools and titanium alloys." — [Academia.edu, Comparative Analysis of SiAlON, CBN & Carbide for Ti (2024)](https://www.academia.edu/114605495/Comparative_Analysis_of_the_Cutting_Performances_of_SiAlON_Ceramic_Cubic_Boron_Nitride_and_Carbide_Cutting_Tools_for_Titanium_Machining)

> "Conventional micron-grain size ceramic tools have not proved better when machining titanium… due to the chemical interactions between the ceramic tools and titanium alloys" — [ABCM COBEM 2007, nano-grain ceramics on Ti-6Al-4V](https://abcm.org.br/anais/cobem/2007/pdf/COBEM2007-0854.pdf)

- Al₂O₃/TiCN ceramic inserts showed "coating peel-off and tool flaking… due to thermal instability at higher cutting speeds" and "higher friction coefficient… which caused substantial temperature rise at tool-tip" — [Sadhana/IASc 2022](https://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/sadh/047/0105).
- "Due to the high reactivity between titanium and most ceramic coatings, together with the low fracture toughness and low thermal conductivity of the coatings, uncoated cemented carbides are frequently used" — [sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1080/17515831.2020.1830251](https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1080/17515831.2020.1830251).
- "Ceramic inserts were also not suitable for single point turning of titanium alloys" — [gala.gre.ac.uk/id/eprint/48453 (Khan 2024)](https://gala.gre.ac.uk/id/eprint/48453/).
- Comparative RSM face-milling study: **carbide outperformed SiAlON and CBN in Ti-6Al-4V (tool life 29 vs. 28 vs. 26 min)** — [Springer IJA-MT 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00170-024-13225-3).
- "Super abrasives like ceramics and cubic boron nitride (CBN) tools are not suitable for machining titanium alloys as low tool life with no economic benefit is achieved because of severe chipping and fracture of the cutting edge" — [Scientific.Net/AMR, doi.org/10.4028/www.scientific.net/amr.1135.234](https://doi.org/10.4028/www.scientific.net/amr.1135.234).
- Classic finding: only "straight" carbide grades survive chemically; most coatings (TiN, TiCN, Al₂O₃) react with the Ti workpiece — Komanduri/Murakoshi conclusions as cited in the [SciELO machinability review](https://www.scielo.org.za).

**Practical tooling spec (a material constraint, identical across all three machines):**

| Class | Suitability | Application |
|---|---|---|
| **Fine-grain uncoated or PVD-coated WC-Co (straight/K-grade, e.g., H13a)** | **Baseline recommendation** | Roughing 30–60 m/min @ 0.3–0.4 mm/rev; finishing 80–120 m/min @ 0.1–0.2 mm/rev ([SciELO](https://www.scielo.org.za); [ISCAR Ti guide](https://www.iscar.com)) |
| **AlTiN-coated carbide end mills** | **Recommended** | Maximum tool life for micro & profile milling — [PMC/NIH, Coated Micro End Mills in Ti-6Al-4V](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6267563/) |
| **AlCrN-coated carbide** | Strong alternative | Chipping resistance |
| **PCD** | Niche, finish-only | Up to ~250 m/min with HPC (3–5× speed gains — [exa.ai library](https://exa.ai/library/publication/42wslbycr85)), but toughness and cost limit it for contoured/interrupted aerospace work |
| **SiAlON ceramic** | Marginal at best | Moderate speeds (<200 m/min) under high-pressure coolant, elevated fracture risk |
| **Al₂O₃ / SiC-whisker ceramic** | **Do not use** | Documented chemical reactivity, chipping, crater wear; surface roughness 5.5 µm vs. 1.6 µm aerospace rejection criteria |
| **CBN** | Not recommended for Ti | Reactivity, rapid wear, no economic benefit |

**High-pressure coolant (HPC) is the single biggest productivity lever** — bigger than any machine-to-machine difference:
- Tool temperature reduced ~25%, flank wear reduced up to ~50% at 70–300 bar directed jets — [journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/09544054JEM2082](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/09544054JEM2082).
- ~70 bar improves chip breaking in Grade 5 ELI turning — [Materials 12-00768 (MDPI)](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/materials/materials-12-00768).
- Through-insert coolant (Kennametal Beyond Blast) gave **2× tool life vs. flood and 25% more than 1,000-psi HPC** in Ti turning at 150 sfm — [mmsonline.com, A Systems Approach for Successful Titanium Machining](https://www.mmsonline.com/articles/a-systems-approach-for-successful-titanium-machining).
- Diminishing/negative returns above ~60–140 bar (edge blast damage) — [exa.ai library](https://exa.ai/library/publication/3p6yqd8bypr).

**Machine implications:** since ceramics (which would demand extreme rigidity at 3–5× cutting speeds) are off the table, prioritize **low-speed torque, damping, and HPC provision** over top spindle rpm. The NLX explicitly documents a "sophisticated spindle labyrinth structure to handle the frequent use of high-pressure coolant" plus spindle air purge ([Lister Machine Tools NLX 2500 data sheet](https://www.listermachinetools.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/pt0uk-nlx2500nd-pdf-data.pdf)) — a durability detail relevant to titanium chip-evacuation environments. HPC availability on the specific Integrex i-400S and Multus U4000 build quotes should be verified **line-item**, and budget **$30–60k installed per machine** for HPC plumbing/filtration as a hidden CAPEX line not covered by base machine price.

---

## 3. Thermal Compensation for ±0.0005" (±12.7 µm)

±0.0005" is at the outer edge of what any of these machines holds *without* active thermal compensation. All three can achieve it **only when** (a) shop ambient is held near ±1 °C (or compensation tolerates the swing), (b) warm-up cycles are observed, and (c) compensation is enabled and tuned. This matters acutely in the Monterrey area, where ambient can swing from ~5 °C winter nights to 40 °C+ summer days.

**DMG MORI NLX 2500 / 2nd Gen — most hardware layers:**
- Coolant circulation through castings (proprietary), ball-screw core cooling, spiral oil jacket around spindle and rotary-tool motor units.
- **Published: thermal displacement 2.0 µm at 3,200 rpm under constant ambient** ([Tuyap NLX 2500 brochure](https://docs.tuyap.online/FDOCS/95474.pdf)).
- Gen 2 "keeps radial displacement within **7 µm even during continuous operation**" with Magnescale MAP offset ([Marketscreener / DMG MORI Sep 2025](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/dmg-mori-launch-of-the-nlx-2500-1250-2nd-generation-br-realize-mx-with-process-integration-aut-ce7d58dfd880f72c)).
- SmartSCALE (MAGNESCALE linear encoders) standard on X, optional X/Y; full closed-loop optional; C-axis index 0.001° (guaranteed 0.003°).

**Mazak Integrex i-400S — adaptive, learning-cycle dependent:**
- Ai Thermal Shield: corrects cutting-edge position as a function of spindle speed, ambient/machine temperature, machine position, and coolant ON/OFF state, and **learns from subsequent measurements** to optimize compensation per environment ([Mazak INTEGREX i NEO Thermal Shield](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/products/integrex-i-neo/); [mazak.com/eu-en/technology/accuracy](https://www.mazak.com/eu-en/technology/accuracy)).
- Standard: spindle temperature-controlled oil jacket + X/Y/Z ball-screw core cooling.
- Quantitative displacement data for the i-400S specifically is **not published**; holding ±12.7 µm requires a stabilized environment, warm-up discipline, and learning-cycle tuning. If evaluating the i NEO successor, request the updated Ai Thermal Shield quantification.

**Okuma Multus U4000 — most independently documented:**
- Thermo-Friendly Concept (TFC): symmetric "manageable deformation" design so growth is predictable and unidirectional; **TAS-S** compensates spindle displacement from temperature + rotation + speed-change + stoppage data; **TAS-C** handles construction/ambient drift ([okuma.co.jp/english/solution_technology/thermo](https://www.okuma.co.jp/english/solution_technology/thermo); [Okuma TFC white paper](https://www.okuma.com/white-paper/thermo-friendly-concepthelps-cnc-machines-take-the-heat)).
- **Published: an 8 °C ambient change produces X-axis 7 µm (∅13 µm), Y-axis 8 µm, Z-axis 9 µm displacement**; suppresses "tilt of the column and milling spindle" during environmental changes ([Okuma MULTUS U brochure](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf)).
- Claimed thermal deformation over time **<10 µm**, "**unrivaled dimensional stability… in normal factory environments with no special measures**," with reduced warm-up time; the concept earned a **Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers award** ([jsme.or.jp](https://www.jsme.or.jp)).
- OSP-P500 adds 0.1 µm control resolution, AbsoScale glass-scale feedback, and an Accuracy Stability Diagnosis that notifies when an accuracy check is actually needed ([OSP-P500 brochure](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/OSP-P500-Brochure_ENGLISH_Mar2023.pdf)); 5-Axis Auto Tuning System re-measures geometric error with a datum sphere and touch probe and auto-sets compensation tables.

**Verdict:** all three can achieve ±12.7 µm per part under disciplined conditions. **Okuma has the strongest published, independently validated thermal-stability data** and the best tolerance of uncontrolled shop environments — directly reducing scrap and dimensional-check frequency. **DMG MORI Gen 2 has the best published quantification for continuous-operation radial displacement (7 µm)** plus linear-encoder feedback independent of ball-screw growth. **Mazak's Ai Thermal Shield is the most adaptive but is learning-cycle dependent and lacks published displacement figures** — treat it as promising, and demand demonstration data on your acceptance test parts.

---

## 4. Siemens NX CAM Integration

All three are supported by NX CAM via **Post Hub / Smart Machine Kit Solutions (SMKS)** — the ecosystem passed a 100-kit milestone, with 170+ license-enabled kits ([Siemens NX Manufacturing blog](https://blogs.sw.siemens.com/nx-manufacturing/smart-machine-kit-solutions-hits-milestone-of-100-kits-on-siemens-post-hub/); [What's new in Post Hub 2024](https://community.sw.siemens.com/s/article/What-s-new-in-Post-Hub-2024)) — but integration depth differs materially:

| Vendor | NX CAM integration depth | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **DMG MORI** | **Deepest, vendor-co-developed.** DMG MORI Digital GmbH builds manufacturer-certified **MTSK (Machine Tool Support Kit)** posts for NX: machine kinematics models + integrated postprocessor + CSE (Cutter Simulation Environment) drivers, including simulation of **DMG MORI technology cycles** — described as "one of a kind — worldwide." Basic and customer-specific adaptation with a dedicated NX support team. Available with SINUMERIK or FANUC controls. ([Siemens DMG MORI postprocessor for NX](https://www.siemens.com/en-us/products/dmg-mori-postprocessor-for-siemens-nx/); [DMG MORI Siemens NX CAD/CAM](https://us.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/work-preparation/cam-software/siemens-nx)) | The decisive advantage for an NX-standardized shop: certified posts, verified kinematics, and in-NX simulation of proprietary cycles. |
| **Mazak** | Supported via Post Hub SMKS (Integrex family models listed); third-party posts also exist for Matrix/SmoothX controls (e.g., CAMdivision, nxcam-postprocessors.com). | Mazak's strategic push is toward its own **MAZATROL Smooth CAM Ai** with digital twin. If your shop standardizes on NX, Mazak works — but the co-engineered depth is DMG MORI's, not Mazak's. |
| **Okuma** | Postprocessor and machine model via Post Hub; Okuma publishes its own free adapter on the **OSP App Store**; OSP-P500 runs full Windows internally, so third-party posts run natively; OSP-P300S/P500 accept standard G-code, easing post development. | Good but least vendor-deep. Best path: OSP-P500 + THINC API + NX with Post Hub postprocessor. |

**Recommendation:** for a shop standardized on Siemens NX, **DMG MORI wins this criterion decisively** — certified posts, kinematics, cycle simulation, and a named support channel remove an entire category of post-processor risk on 5-axis mill-turn code. Mazak and Okuma are workable via Post Hub but require more in-house or integrator effort to reach equivalent confidence.

## 5. AS9100D Traceability via MTConnect / OPC-UA

All three deliver compliant data paths; the differentiators are standardization depth, tool-genealogy formalization, and cybersecurity.

**DMG MORI — most open and standards-aligned:**
- **IoT Connector standard on every new machine from 2020**, supporting **OPC-UA, MTConnect and MQTT simultaneously** ([DMG MORI Connectivity](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/connectivity)); "MDC: Standardized machine data output in OPC UA, MTconnect and MQTT formats" stated explicitly on the NLX 2500 page ([dmgmori.com NLX 2500 Control & Software](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)).
- **CELOS X Tool Master + Tool Data Exchange (TDE)** transfers tool identity via **OPC UA**, creating a per-tool, per-cutting-edge digital chain of custody — directly supports **AS9100D §8.5.2 (identification & traceability)** ([DMG MORI Tool Master](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/celos-x/celos-x-tool-master)).
- Active in **umati** (OPC-UA Companion Specification for machine tools) and Factory-X; IoT connector retrofit for machines up to 10 years old; IoT connector flex for third-party machines; NETservice remote diagnostics.

**Mazak — strongest cybersecurity posture:**
- **All Mazak machines ship MTConnect-capable** ([Mazak USA MTConnect](https://www.mazakusa.com/machines/technology/digital-solutions/mtconnect)).
- **SmartBox 2.0 (Sep 2024)** adds **MQTT and OPC UA** on top of MTConnect, with industrial-grade edge compute and advanced cybersecurity, up to 10 machines per box ([Mazak press release, Sep 2024](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/news-media/news/mazak-advances-machine-connectivity-smart-box-2/)); SENSOR BOX variants cover non-MTConnect legacy machines.
- MAZATROL SmoothAi manages production data including "all parameters required for machining as well as traceability" ([mazak.com traceability](https://www.mazak.com)); OEM-to-OEM MTConnect agents at [mtconnect.mazakcorp.com](http://mtconnect.mazakcorp.com/).

**Okuma — most turnkey traceability, most open platform:**
- **MTConnect agent free via the OSP App Store** — Windows-based control, no external box needed ([Okuma MTConnect](https://www.okuma.com/mtconnect); [ThingConnect Okuma guide](https://thingconnect.io/integrations/machine-brands/okuma)).
- **OSP-P500M / OSP-P700A add a factory-installed OPC-UA server** built to the OPC Foundation CNC information model (the umati standard), with communication encryption per Okuma's P500 cybersecurity release ([Okuma Europe, Jun 2023](https://www.okuma.eu/newsroom/press-releases/detail/next-generation-cnc-control/)). **Caution:** on other OSP variants, OPC-UA requires third-party add-ons (e.g., CNCnetPDM) — confirm the control variant and OPC-UA line-item in the quotation.
- **Connect Plan** with **Machining Record Management** ties individual workpiece ID to machining and gauging results — "Who, when, where, and what kind of machining was done, and the gauging results obtained, can be easily checked" — with automatic archival supporting **AS9100D §7.5.3 (records) and §8.5 (production)** ([Okuma Connect Plan](https://www.okuma.com/connect-plan)). Machine Data Logger (optional) accumulates spindle load, axis load, override, and external sensor data. Okuma explicitly targets "industries with a strong need for robust data collection and the need to meet traceability requirements, such as aerospace manufacturers."

**Verdict:** for a new MES/QMS build, **DMG MORI's open architecture (OPC-UA + MTConnect + MQTT standard) is the most flexible**, with the most formalized tool-data lineage via TDE. **Okuma's Connect Plan is the most turnkey out-of-box** for aerospace part genealogy. **Mazak's SmartBox 2.0 has the strongest cybersecurity posture** — relevant to AS9100D records integrity and ITAR-adjacent customer audits — but the box is an accessory purchase.
